answer: Higher temperature makes the particles move faster, so they collide more often, and a much larger fraction of the collisions have energy at or above the activation energy, so more collisions are successful. Higher concentration packs more reactant particles into the same volume, so collisions happen more frequently per second and the rate goes up.

(a) HSO4⁻ is the Brønsted-Lowry acid because it donates a proton; H2O is the base because it accepts the proton. (b) SO4²⁻ is the conjugate base of HSO4⁻ and H3O⁺ is the conjugate acid of H2O. (c) The pairs are HSO4⁻ / SO4²⁻ and H2O / H3O⁺. (d) The claim is wrong because in this reaction water accepts a proton, so it is acting as a base.

(i) The reaction is exothermic, so thermal energy behaves like a product. Raising the temperature adds thermal energy and the system shifts left, toward the reactants, to use it up. Because the temperature changed, K itself decreases. (ii) At constant temperature, decreasing the volume raises the pressure. The system shifts right toward NH3 because there are 2 moles of gas on the right and 4 on the left. K does not change, because only a temperature change changes K. (iii) A catalyst speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the position of equilibrium and K are both unchanged; equilibrium is just reached faster.

(a) The center-of-mass velocity stays the same. The spring force is internal to the two-cart system, so the system's momentum is conserved and the center of mass keeps moving exactly as it was. (b) Momentum is conserved, so the two carts receive equal and opposite changes in momentum. The lighter cart ends up moving faster.

(a) Independent variable: the initial speed of the block. Dependent variable: the distance it slides before stopping. Control: use the same block on the same surface for every trial. (b) Friction does work −μk·m·g·d on the block, and that work removes all of its kinetic energy: ½·m·v0² = μk·m·g·d, so μk = v0² / (2·g·d).

(a) The solid sphere reaches the bottom first. Its rotational inertia, (2/5)MR², is smaller than the shell's, (2/3)MR², so at any given translational speed a smaller share of its energy is tied up in rotation. More of the gravitational energy goes into translation, so it accelerates faster down the incline. (b) From energy conservation, Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω² with ω = v/R, which gives v² = 2gh / [1 + I/(MR²)]. The solid sphere has the smaller I/(MR²), so it has the greater translational speed at the bottom for the same drop.

(a) The parameter is p, the proportion of all students at the school who support a later start time. p̂ = 84/120 = 0.70. (b) Random: we have to assume the 120 students were a random sample. 10%: 120 is less than 10% of all students. Large counts: 84 successes and 36 failures are both at least 10. (c) 0.70 ± 1.96 × √(0.70 × 0.30 / 120) = 0.70 ± 0.082, so the interval is (0.618, 0.782). (d) We are 95% confident that between 61.8% and 78.2% of students support a later start time, so about 95% of students fall in that range.

(a) For x > 1, (x² + 2x − 3)/(x − 1) = (x + 3)(x − 1)/(x − 1) = x + 3, so lim(x→1⁺) f(x) = 4. (b) For continuity the left-hand limit must equal the right-hand limit: k(1) + 2 = 4, so k = 2. Then f(1) = m must equal the limit, so m = 4. (c) With k = 3 and m = 4, the left-hand limit is 3 + 2 = 5 and the right-hand limit is 4, so the limit does not exist and f is not continuous at x = 1.
